quotes.label: Cottage Opening/Window
quotes.quote: In rural Germany, the Monster takes shelter near a small cottage. In the cottage he watches the cottagers, learning about language and human history. Nietzsche defines truth as when “man perceives that his world has been devised only for the purpose of meeting certain psychological needs, and that he has no right whatsoever to it” (Nietzsche 17).
quotes.analysis: While the monster is observing the cottagers, the Monster’s pursuit of knowledge, instead of bringing him closer to acceptance, leaves him with the understanding of his inability to fit into the world, losing his sense of Truth.

quotes.label: The cottagers’ table
quotes.quote: The Monster describes learning language as opening “a wide field for wonder and delight” for him,
quotes.analysis: demonstrating the Monster’s hope that knowledge will lead him to acceptance among the humans (Shelley 84).

quotes.label: The reflection of the Monster’s face in the puddle.
quotes.quote: However, as he learns that there is no one like him, he questions whether he is “a monster, a blot upon the earth from which all men fled and whom all men disowned” (Shelley 85).
quotes.analysis: This disconnect highlights how the Monsters newfound knowledge caused the realization of being an outcast.

quotes.label: The open book
quotes.quote: The Monster then relates the “agony that [those] reflections” caused him and that his “sorrow only increased with knowledge” (Shelley 85).
quotes.analysis: The Monster’s realization that his quest for learning has only led him to more pain reveals his withering faith in an objective Truth worth searching for.

quotes.label: The lichen-covered rock
quotes.quote: The Monster then finishes his loss of faith in Truth, by claiming that knowledge “clings to the mind when it has once seized on it like a lichen on the rock” and wishing to “shake off all thought and feeling” (Shelley 85).
quotes.analysis: Describing knowledge with words like “clings” and “seized” convey a parasitic notion that highlights the Monster’s new disdain for acquiring knowledge. Him wishing to no longer think or feel highlights his abandonment of searching for knowledge, revealing his collapse of Truth.
